title: Differential Forms As Measurements
notes: Open the lecture by reframing forms as measurement devices rather than decorative dx notation. The ladder is the route for the hour: first a covector measures tangent directions, then smooth fields of covectors pull back through maps, multiply by wedges, differentiate intrinsically, and finally interact with flows through Lie derivative and contraction.

title: Cotangent Measurements
notes: Spend time separating tangent vectors from covectors. A tangent basis changes like vectors, while the dual basis must change oppositely so the evaluation pairing stays fixed. The inverse-transpose matrix is not a trick; it is exactly the algebra needed to keep epsilon i of e j equal to delta ij after a frame change.

title: Differentials Of Functions
notes: Use the contour picture to make df tangible. A vector tangent to a level curve gives zero measurement, while a vector crossing contours gives the directional derivative. Stress that df is defined without a metric. Calling it a gradient already assumes extra structure that the chapter has not chosen.

title: Smooth One-Forms
notes: Move from a single cotangent space to a field of covectors. In a chart, smoothness is inspected through the coefficient functions a i, but the object is global because coordinate changes transform the basis and the coefficients together. This is the first place where local notation and invariant meaning have to be held at once.

title: Pullback Of One-Forms
notes: Pullback is the central functorial move for forms. A vector in the source is pushed forward just long enough for the target covector to evaluate it, and the resulting number is recorded back at the source. The coordinate rule is the Jacobian-transpose rule, which matches the notebook check for the curved map.

title: Restriction Is Inclusion Pullback
notes: Restriction should not be presented as a separate ad hoc operation. If a submanifold sits inside M by an inclusion i, then a form restricts by pulling back along i. This explains why only tangent directions to the submanifold are tested and why ambient normal information disappears automatically.

title: Differential K-Forms
notes: Generalize the measurement picture from one input to k inputs. Alternation means the form is sensitive to oriented k-dimensional content: swapping two directions reverses sign and repeating a direction kills the measurement. The local basis dx I is compact notation for ordered wedges of coordinate covectors.

title: Wedge Sign Ledger
notes: Treat the wedge product as signed bookkeeping for alternating measurements. Students often memorize dy wedge dx equals minus dx wedge dy but miss the structural reason: to move a degree k form past a degree l form, k times l swaps are needed. The ledger makes repeated basis factors vanish visibly.

title: The Circle Form
notes: This example ties several operations together in one familiar manifold. The ambient one-form minus y dx plus x dy restricts to the angular measurement on the unit circle. Pulling back by the standard parametrization produces dt, so the integral over one turn is 2 pi, even though no global single-valued angle function exists on the circle.

title: Invariant Forms On Lie Groups
notes: Use the circle as the concrete Lie group before naming the general construction. A covector chosen at the identity can be transported by left translations to every group element, producing a left-invariant form. The point is that group multiplication supplies a canonical way to compare tangent spaces.

title: Exterior Derivative In A Chart
notes: Introduce d as the degree-one operator that differentiates coefficients and then wedges with the coordinate basis already present. The local formula is computational, not merely local decoration. It gives students a way to compute d omega while later properties explain why the answer is independent of the chosen chart.

title: Why D Squared Is Zero
notes: The cancellation is the heart of the operator. Applying d twice differentiates mixed partials in both orders, and the wedge sign places them with opposite signs. Under the usual smoothness assumptions the mixed partials agree, so the coefficient cancels. The notebook check records this as a zero three-form coefficient.

title: Locality Gives A Global Operator
notes: This slide is about trust in the construction. The formula for d is written in coordinates, but it is local and compatible on overlaps, so the pieces glue. The uniqueness statement matters pedagogically: any operator with the listed behavior on functions and products must be the exterior derivative.

title: Pullback Commutes With D
notes: Now connect the two main operations. Pullback respects functions, wedge products, and exterior derivative, so computations can move to whichever manifold has the easier coordinates. This is why parametrizations are so powerful: the circle period was computed by pulling the form back to the line.

title: Lie Derivative And Flow
notes: The Lie derivative measures infinitesimal change along a vector field by pulling tensors back along the flow and differentiating at time zero. For functions it recovers directional derivative. For vector fields it recovers the bracket, which measures the failure of the two infinitesimal motions to commute.

title: Interior Multiplication And Cartan
notes: Interior multiplication inserts a vector field into the first slot of a form, lowering degree by one. Cartan's formula is the key bridge: flow change equals contraction after exterior differentiation plus exterior differentiation after contraction. The residual check is useful because it confirms equality at the coefficient level in a concrete example.

title: Global Formula And Recap
notes: End by showing that the exterior derivative can be written without coordinates using vector fields and Lie brackets. The first sum differentiates the form value along each vector field, while the second sum corrects for the fact that the vector fields themselves vary and may not commute. Then recap the whole ladder from measurement to Cartan.
